en: Commentary on the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty Commentary composed by the Śramaṇa Jingmai of the Great Ci’en Monastery, Tang Dynasty
Now, the ultimate principle is profound and subtle; the traces of cognition are extinguished in stillness. The five eyes serve as an impartial mirror, and the four wisdoms are but dimly heard.

How could one entrust the mystery to silence while ill, or manifest the wondrous through non-speaking at the time of passing away? Nevertheless, although the ultimate truth and conventional reality differ, [they are ultimately one].

The signless is not different [from itself]. Movement and stillness are thus separated; that which transcends words is identical. Identity has never begun as difference; difference has never begun as identity.
Since identity and difference have never begun, identity makes identity and difference identical; since identity and difference have never begun, difference makes difference and identity different.

Difference, by its own nature, is different from difference; difference is not different from identity. Identity, by its own nature, is identical to identity; identity is not identical to difference. Thus, identity and difference have never been one.

The ultimate and the conventional are not inherently different; yet those who are deluded claim that when they are said to be the same, it means their differences are identical, and when they are said to be different, it means their sameness is distinct.
Thus, through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), they increase what does not exist, and through the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), they diminish what truly is.

This causes [delusion] to flow like a great torrent of water, destroying and submerging all things, while the fire of confusion blazes fiercely, scorching all classes of beings. Only the Unsurpassed...
O Dharma King! You wish to dispel these celestial calamities, turning the round mirror to illuminate the hidden depths and brightening the great light within the profound darkness.

Thus, you cause the objective realm not to obstruct the mind, and the mind to be free from entanglement with the realm. When the realm does not obstruct the mind, the realm is devoid of marks (*nimitta*).
When the mind is free from entanglement with the realm, the mind is not a subject of vision. Therefore, the Perfected One employs the wondrous wisdom of non-vision to illumine the...
Regarding the true realm of marks: the mind and its objects have never been different, yet the conditions and their illumination have never been the same.

One must eliminate the myriad attachments of stagnant emotions and level the distinctions between self and other within accumulated thoughts. Is this not where the unsurpassed divine mantra resides? That which is called Prajñā—
"Pure Wisdom" (Jìng huì) is the Chinese translation for *prajñā*. "Pāra" means "the other shore" (*pāra*) in Chinese. "Mita" is translated as "to reach" (*mita*).

However, as for wisdom and the shore, their names and characteristics are fundamentally submerged in the ultimate; how could there be any further distinction between defilement and purity, or this and that?
These terms are merely used to praise *prajñā* by way of metaphorical expression. Because it is far removed from all extremes, it is therefore called "mind. Thus, the Sūtra says:
Just as the mind-consciousness of sentient beings exists in substance, yet lacks characteristics such as length, shortness, blue, or yellow;
it is further said that this body is a city, with the mind-king dwelling within it. Therefore, we now cite it to reveal its central reality.
However, it is named "Wisdom" (Hui) because it exhausts all illumination; it is titled "The Shore" (An) because it reaches the ultimate limit of merit; and it is called "Mind" (Xin)...
To provide for the eyes is to exhaust their reality; if illumination were not exhaustive, it would be insufficient to clarify the Great Radiance within all-encompassing awakening.

If merit were not ultimate, it could not yet open the dark chamber within the Mysterious Capital. If reality were not inexhaustible, how could one profoundly unify existence and non-existence, or the true and the conventional?
Its phrasing is concise yet its meaning is comprehensive; its diction is brilliant and its purport is subtle, encompassing the multitude.
Its profound subtleties encompass the dark pivot of the myriad scriptures; thus, the Tripitaka masters have cherished its flavor within their hearts.

Though it has traveled across vast distances, they rely upon it to remain free from entanglement. Although this was previously translated, as I have reviewed the extant texts, I now retranslate it so that there may be no further confusion.
Having set my mind upon learning, I began to recite and uphold it; even now, at sixty years of age, I dare not grow negligent.

Out of admiration and with a heart of reverent devotion, I have briefly set forth my humble reflections. This is not intended to transmit the lamp of the Dharma, but rather to seek the ferry of the future.
In order to explicate this sutra, I shall provide a brief analysis in four sections: first, clarifying why it begins with "Thus" and ends without the "Practice" section;
second, clarifying the intent of teaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*; third, clarifying the fundamental tenets of the teaching; and fourth, analyzing the textual divisions.
Commentary:
First, it clarifies why the beginning lacks the phrase "Thus" (evam) and the end lacks the statement regarding "practice. Question:

Upon examining the sublime words of the profound scriptures, there is no difference among the various sutras; they all place the statement "Thus" at the outset and conclude with the words regarding "practice. Consequently...
If one studies these in detail, one will achieve perfect harmony; thus the inexhaustible lamp shall shine forever.
For this reason, even at the conclusion of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, this person was still burdened with the task of clarifying the *Sūtras*, and thus composed verses on this principle.

Yet, in the present ultimate canon (*paramārtha-śāstra*), there is no such discourse at the beginning, nor is there any statement regarding its practice at the end. What is the reason for this? Answer: To examine the origin of the Dharma at the Deer Park...
The profound and subtle texts had not yet been spread upon the bamboo slips; when the Crane Forest (Śrāvastī) closed its gates, the multitude of sages were finally inscribed upon the golden scrolls.
Thus, the eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma produced rare melodies throughout the Five Regions, and the twelve true expositions struck at the profound purport across the nine realms of existence.
Now, as for the comprehensive synthesis of all scriptures, their grand framework is twofold: first, the collection of various assemblies of teachings.
In texts such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Āgamas*, which consist of compilations from multiple assemblies, there is at the beginning "Thus [have I heard]" and at the end "fully practiced.

In other scriptures concerning the conduct of practitioners, some are derived from sūtras of multiple assemblies and thus have "Thus" at the beginning and "fully practiced" at the end, such as the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika*.
Others are derived from sūtras of a single assembly and thus lack "Thus" at the beginning, yet [end with]... at the conclusion.
It lacks the "Observance of the Teachings," such as those found in the *Avalokiteśvara-śāsana* and other texts.
This present sutra, having flowed from a single assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, likewise begins without such [invocations] and ends with the omission of the "Observance of the Teachings."
The second section clarifies the intent behind teaching Prajñāpāramitā. This intent is to dismantle the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Now, the reason why sentient beings are obstructed by the mountains of defilement and submerged in the ocean of afflictions and delusions is none other than the burden of pervasive conceptualization regarding persons and phenomena.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "Some say that all things arise from Maheśvara..."
They are born as Brahmā, or born from Viṣṇu, or born from the primordial nature (prakṛti), or born spontaneously; they propound various views concerning a self and what belongs to a self.
Thus, through these and other immeasurable erroneous attachments, they fall into views of no-cause, false causes, nihilism, eternalism, and so forth, remaining ignorant of the True Dharma.
Desiring to sever such false views and cause them to understand the Buddha-dharma, [the Buddha taught this].
The characteristics of dependent origination are explained by means of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
that is to say, all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, being ultimately empty and non-existent, as taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. As the Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as being like space, inexhaustible. Since one wishes to employ the Mahāyāna Dharma...

The characteristics of causes and conditions are explained. The characteristics of causes and conditions consist of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
In these two natures, all mental and verbal characteristics are forever absent;

yet, sentient beings, deluded by their inversions, wander in error therein, giving rise to the pervasive conceptualization of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-parikalpita*). However, that which is thus conceptualized is fundamentally non-existent. Therefore—
It is said that what is neither born nor extinguished is ultimately empty and non-existent. Question:

While the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) may indeed be a causal condition (*pratyaya*), how can the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) also be called a causal condition? Answer: Because it is explained through the gateway of causal conditions for the sake of clarifying its meaning;

although suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are [ultimately unconditioned], they are also spoken of as causal conditions, because the perfected nature is not separate from causal conditions.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason and by what causes and conditions is the Prajñā taught?
For example, neither Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, nor the great earth, is moved without cause or by minor circumstances. Now, for what great matter does the Buddha teach the Prajñā?
The answer is: "It is because he wishes to proclaim the bodhisattva practices, and in order to respond to the Brahma King."
Because of what was previously requested, and in order to sever the various knots of doubt among sentient beings—

beings who have, since beginningless time, been afflicted and disturbed by the diseases of the fetters (saṃyojana) and for whom no healer has appeared, and who are constantly led astray by the false teachers of external paths—
the Buddha, as the King of Physicians, preaches the medicine of Prajñā to treat them, in order to extract those multitudes from their suffering.
It is for the sake of causing those such as Śāriputra to emerge from the two extremes and enter the Middle Way that the Prajñā is taught.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of generating faith in the Buddha-dharma among those such as the brahmin Dīrghanakha; and it is for the sake of explaining the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
It is for the sake of various great matters such as these that the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is taught.
Third, the clarification of the fundamental tenet of this teaching: it takes the *prajñā* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its tenet.

*Prajñā* is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while true reality is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is absolutely non-existent, like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;
therefore, the Sūtra says: "Unarisen and unceasing, ultimately empty and peerless. [This refers to] the dependent nature...

Arising-nature exists according to conventional truth, but does not exist according to ultimate truth. Although it is said to exist conventionally, its nature, characteristics, and names are ultimately non-existent.
As for ultimate nature, the nature and characteristics of mind and speech are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning; this is taught in order to dispel conventional existence.
One relies upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to eliminate [conventional existence]. Once the conventional has been leveled, the ultimate also vanishes.

These two natures can be merged through wisdom (*jñāna*), but they are difficult to fathom with ordinary sentiment (*citta*). Therefore, the sphere of the true mark of *prajñā* is equal. Now, phenomena transcend all objective spheres, and the Sage extinguishes all forms of cognition.
Because he transcends all objective spheres, there are no external conditions; because he extinguishes all [cognitions], [he is free from internal conceptualization].
Because of this knowledge, there is no grasping within and no conditioning without. When there is no grasping within, then both the internal and external are darkened in stillness;
mind and object are simultaneously quiescent. What, then, could be relied upon as either the ultimate or the conventional? If one wishes to say it exists, it has no appearance and no form.

If one wishes to say that it is non-existent, the Sage is enlightened by means of it. Indeed, to speak of the "suchness" (tathatā) of the ultimate and conventional, the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi), "dharma-nature" (dharmatā), or "true mark" (lakṣaṇa) is merely a forced designation.

Regarding the textual explanation of the fourth section, this passage is divided into two parts: first, the brief; second, the detailed. [The brief: *Note: The provided text fragment ends with "略" (brief). The translation reflects the structure of the commentary up to that point.*

Within this, there are four sections. First, it clarifies the practitioner who engages in cultivation. Second, from "Practicing profound *prajñā*" onwards, it clarifies the wisdom of responsive application.

Third, from "Seeing clearly the five aggregates" onwards, it clarifies the realm of realization and verification. Fourth, from "Crossing over all suffering and distress" onwards, it clarifies the perfection of principle and the attainment of the fruit.
Second, from "Śāriputra," onwards, there is a further detailed analysis.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, within this concise explanation, we first clarify the meaning of the "practitioner.

To speak of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is to refer to the general virtue shared by all great beings (mahāsattvas) who have attained the stages (bhūmis) and above; it does not refer exclusively to Amitābha.
This is its left-hand support. How is this clarified? This method of cultivation appears within the "Chapter on Practice and Response" (*Pratipatty-abhisamaya*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Therein, the Buddha addresses Śāriputra, clarifying that when bodhisattvas practice prajñā, they should contemplate the bodhisattva and the Buddha’s prajñā, as well as the five aggregates and all other phenomena, as being merely names—just like the self.
Sentient beings are all unapprehendable because they are empty. This is called the practice of Prajñā by a Bodhisattva who has entered the stages;
one should contemplate and observe that all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, exist only as names provisionally established in accordance with worldly convention.
Ultimately, there are no true or conventional natures or characteristics. For the characteristics of all phenomena are merely...
Because that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*) is ultimately empty, by forming this understanding, one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma*).
Since there is no obstruction regarding any object, one is called "Avalokiteśvara. The old translation says "Guanshiyin" (Contemplator of the World's Sounds).
"Sound" (*yin*) refers precisely to sounds and names; it means contemplating that all phenomena possess nothing more than sounds and names established as conventional designations.
...and that is all. Question: How is it known that one who practices these exercises is a bodhisattva who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), rather than one who is still prior to the stages?
Answer: According to the scriptural calculations, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one surpasses all others except for the Buddha’s own wisdom;
therefore, it is clear that this is not the stage prior to the *bhūmis*. The term "bodhisattva" is abbreviated here; if expressed in its full Sanskrit form, [it would be *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*].
One should say *bodhisattva mahāsattva*. *Bodhi* is translated in the Tang language as "awakening" (*jue*).

To translate it as "the Way" (*dao*) is an error. Question: Since *buddha* is also called "awakening" in the Tang language, using *bodhi* to mean "the Way" would result in no confusion between the two terms; this seems to hit the mark. Why do you call it an error? Answer:

The term *buddha* refers to the one who is capable of realizing awakening. Thus, the two names do not overlap. It is for this reason that [the distinction] is maintained. Why do you say it is an error?
One does not grasp at awakening (*bodhi*). Awakening merely grasps that which is capable of realizing it. Regarding the phrase "does not grasp at":
although the name "awakening" is the same, the wisdom of the "one who [grasps]" is not identical. How could the awakening of *bodhi* be translated by means of the awakening of the *mārga* (path)?
Therefore, the ultimate truth resides in the fruit; having already discerned these errors, they were exposed in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*. Is this not something one should believe?
*Sattva* is translated in Chinese as *yǒuqíng* (sentient being). The old translation *zhòngshēng* (multitude of beings) is erroneous.
*Bhujyuṣaṇa* is translated as *zhòngshēng* (multitude of beings) or *yǒuqíng* (sentient being); these Sanskrit terms are entirely distinct and must not be confused in translation.

*Mahā* means "great. *Sattva* means "sentient being. Thus, it refers to a "Great Sentient Being who is awakened" (*bodhisattva*). "Awakened" (*bodhi*) is that which is sought; "sentient being" (*sattva*) is...

"Capable of seeking" refers to those who possess awakening; this term applies generally to all three vehicles. Therefore, it is distinguished by the prefix "Great" (*mahā*) to indicate that these are not bodhisattvas who seek the awakening of the middle or lower vehicles.
Furthermore, "awakening" (*bodhi*) is the objective sought, while "sentient being" (*sattva*) is the object for whom one acts.
This means they possess great vows for both self and others, seeking sublime awakening in order to benefit sentient beings. Moreover, *sattva*...

This is the meaning of "valiant. Because one seeks great enlightenment with courageous diligence, one is called a *bodhisattva*. Now, for the sake of brevity in this context, the syllable *ti* is removed from *bodhi* and the syllable *tta* is removed from *sattva*; thus, one simply says "Bodhisattva. This term applies to all stages. However, when referring specifically to those on the stages (*bhūmi*), one should say "Mahāsattva. As for why this is not mentioned in the text: [The remainder of the passage follows: ...because it is intended to apply to the stage of faith and so forth, and because the term "Bodhisattva" is sufficient to encompass all [stages] from the first aspiration up to the ultimate fruit. Furthermore, since the term "Bodhisattva" is well-known in the world, it is used here to avoid confusion. It is also because the term "Mahāsattva" is reserved for those who have attained the irreversible stage (*avaivartika*). Therefore, although the term "Mahāsattva" is appropriate for the stages, the text uses "Bodhisattva" to indicate that this person is capable of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, it is said: "One who possesses the three kinds of courage is called a Bodhisattva. What are these three? First, the courage to seek the path; second, the courage to practice the path; and third, the courage to attain the fruit. One who possesses these three is named a Bodhisattva. This is the meaning of the term. It is also because he is a being (*sattva*) who has set out for enlightenment (*bodhi*). Therefore, he is called a Bodhisattva. This is the general definition. Regarding the specific distinctions: there are four types of Bodhisattvas based on their faculties—those of dull faculties, middling faculties, sharp faculties, and those of supreme faculties. There are also four types based on their lineage—those of the Śrāvaka lineage, the Pratyekabuddha lineage, the Buddha lineage, and those of indeterminate lineage. There are also four types based on their stage—those in the stage of faith, those in the stage of practice, those in the stage of seeing, and those in the stage of cultivation. There are also four types based on their attainment—those who have not yet entered the stages, those who have entered the stages, those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship, and those who have attained the fruit of Buddhahood. Among these, the Bodhisattva spoken of here is one who has generated the mind of enlightenment and is practicing the path; therefore, the term "Bodhisattva" is used. This concludes the explanation of the term. Now, as for the phrase "for the sake of this direction": it means that in order to conform to the linguistic conventions of this region, the abbreviated form is employed. This is the reason for the usage. Thus ends the section on the etymological explanation of the term "Bodhisattva. Now, to summarize: the term "Bodhisattva" is established based on the union of the two meanings of "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) and "being" (*sattva*). When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the second [section] clarifies the wisdom of cultivation and application.
Regarding the phrase "practicing the profound *prajñā*": the Great Illumination is signless (*animitta*) and wondrous.
Wisdom is without cognition. Because it is signless, all signs have already dissolved; that which is characterized cannot characterize it.

Because it is without cognition, all objects of knowledge are extinguished; that which is known cannot know it. Although that which is known cannot know it, the profound luminosity of the perfect mirror remains.

The mirror reflects the ultimate Dharma-realm; though its marks cannot be characterized by marks, it disperses reflections throughout the three thousandfold world-system and manifests forms within the ten thousand phenomena.
This may be called "taking form within the unknowing. Since it can take form within the unknowing, how could it be measured by the capacity of knowing?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva practices Prajñā, he does not think, 'I am practicing Prajñā. He does not...

One practices *prajñā*; it is not that one does not practice *prajñā*. When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they are able to bring benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, yet they do not even conceive the thought that there is such benefit. Why is this?

It is because this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that exists apart from the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*). Practicing *prajñā* in this manner is the most foremost, the most honored, and the most supreme.
It is unsurpassed; is it not fitting that it be profound?
It clearly perceives that the five aggregates and so forth are all empty (the character "equal" [等] appears in both this commentary and Master Ji’s *Youzan*; it is absent in other editions).
The third clarifies the realm of realized realization. Regarding the statement, "to perceive that the five aggregates and so forth are all empty":

form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called the five aggregates. The phrase "and so forth" includes the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the four noble truths.
These five categories are all empty; therefore, it says they are "all empty. Now, these five aggregates are all pervasive.

Because causes and effects are all gathered together and formed by bearing various phenomena, they are collectively termed "aggregates" (*skandha*). This refers merely to the matter of gathering and bearing.

Various heterodox teachers falsely cling to these five types as each having a substantial entity, and furthermore, they calculate that there exists a self (*ātman*) that exercises sovereign control over them, whether identical to or separate from the five. Now, when it is said that "all are empty," it means:
The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of each of the aggregates (*skandha*) possesses a substantial reality; this clinging is entirely empty.

Furthermore, whether in identity with or separate from these five [aggregates], the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are empty. This is why it is said they are "all" [empty]. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"One does not perceive form (*rūpa*) as having the characteristic of arising, the characteristic of ceasing, the characteristic of defilement, or the characteristic of purity; and so it is for consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well. Such is its nature."
Because they are empty. It is further said: "One does not see form conjoined with feeling, nor even one sees formations conjoined with consciousness.
Why? Because there is no dharma that is conjoined with non-dharma; their nature is empty. This clarifies that both types of grasping are empty.
Within emptiness, how could there be arising and ceasing, or conjunction and non-conjunction?
It delivers one from all suffering and calamity.

The fourth [point] clarifies that the principle is perfected and the fruit is realized. Regarding the phrase "delivering from all suffering," this clarifies the fruit of *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

This means that because one realizes the emptiness of the fruit of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one is able to deliver oneself from the fruit of the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and attain [liberation].
This refers to *nirvāṇa with remainder*. The phrase "crossing over all calamities" clarifies the fruit of *nirvāṇa with remainder*.
That is to say, because one realizes that the cause of the five aggregates is empty, one thereby crosses over all calamities, such as the torrents [of saṃsāra] and the bonds of afflictions.
This term "calamity" (āpad) refers generally to all afflictions (*kleśa*), as they are all capable of binding and obstructing sentient beings; it does not refer solely to the four calamities.
Thus, when one realizes that both the aggregates (*skandha*) and their causes and effects are empty, this is called *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is synonymous with liberation (*vimukti*).
Emptiness and the other [three seals] are the gates to liberation. Once these gates are established, suffering and calamity are thereby exhausted, which constitutes the direct realization.
This is liberation. Question: Those who enter *nirvāṇa* do so universally by means of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Why then do you speak only of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? Answer: When there is no grasping or rejection with which to contend, that is the Great Dharma. Now, because it is empty, it is signless; because it is signless, it is wishless.
Since one has already spoken of emptiness, all phenomena are profoundly identical; why worry about the two [other gates] not being empty? Furthermore...
This can be understood from the fact that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is primary. For one who is born dependent upon karma, birth is extinguished by relying on emptiness;
the principle is obscured by afflictions, yet once delusion ceases, the principle becomes manifest. Now that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are empty, suffering and calamity are transcended.
It is for this reason that one accords with this ultimate cessation (*nirodha*). Thus it is so.
From this point downward is the second section, which extensively elucidates *prajñā*. This passage also consists of four parts: first, elucidating *prajñā* by means of dispelling attachments;
second, from "Because there is nothing to be apprehended" (*anupalambhāt*) onwards, elucidating *prajñā* by means of attaining the fruit of realization;

third, from "Therefore, know that *prajñā*" onwards, extensively praising and manifesting its excellence; and fourth, from "Then he spoke the mantra" onwards, reiterating the preceding sutra and manifesting [the truth] by means of the mantra.
Victorious!
In the first section, which clarifies *prajñā* by means of dispelling attachments, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that all objects of attachment are empty;

second, from "there is no wisdom and no attainment" onwards, it clarifies that the subject who realizes [emptiness] is also empty. Within the clarification that the objects of attachment are empty, [it concerns] phenomena (*dharma*).
The gates are immeasurable; for now, however, we shall dispel them by means of five gates. What are these five? First, the emptiness of the five aggregates (*skandha*);

second, the emptiness of the twelve bases (*āyatana*); third, the emptiness of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); fourth, the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
and fifth, the emptiness of the four noble truths (*satya*). The text that dispels these five gates consists of five sections. Within each of these, one by one—
Section. All [of these] universally eliminate both types of person and phenomena that are conceptually imputed, as has already been analyzed above.

First, emptiness is elucidated by means of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). This passage consists of three parts: first, the explanation of the reason why the preceding aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭiskandha*) is empty;
second, from "Śāriputra" onwards, the explanation of the basis for the preceding phrase "crossing over all suffering and calamity"; third, is...
Therefore, below, the initial category is cited after the latter.
Regarding the mention of "Śāriputra" in the preceding section: he is the interlocutor responding to the teaching. According to the original Sanskrit manuscript, it should be written as "Śāri."
"Pitara. "Śarī" is the name of a bird; the old translations rendered it as "mynah" (kū-ku-p'uk) or "body" (shen). The Tripiṭaka Master says that neither is correct.
The śarī bird is actually the spring oriole; it resembles the mynah in appearance. However, this bird is extremely clever and wise;
its vocalizations shift and transform with complete mastery and freedom, such that among all other birds, none can surpass it.
Furthermore, in this region, the names for this bird vary and are not uniform; thus, it cannot be definitively rendered by a single name, and so its original sound has been retained.
*Putra* (弗怛羅) means "son" in the language of Tang, and so it has been translated as such.
*Śāri* (舍利) is the name of its mother; she was by nature intelligent, quick-witted, and eloquent. To use the standards of the country of India to compare her—

He was named after the nightingale (*kuling*). His mother was previously a woman of talent and wisdom; although she surpassed others in her own right, when she debated with her elder brother, Gouzhiluo, she was always bested by him.

However, once she conceived this son, her brother was constantly defeated. By the time the boy reached the age of eight, there were no masters of debate from any land who could rival him in discourse.
At that time, people remarked that while his mother had been brilliant, now it was the son...

Furthermore, in order to manifest that the mother and son were both exceptionally intelligent and that their wisdom surpassed all other sages, he used the mother’s honorable title to formally signal her renown.
Question: What has been refuted and what has been revealed here? When attachments are exhausted and principles are made manifest, this is truly the office of a Great Being (Mahāsattva).

This is not the concern of those engaged in minor studies. Now, you have summoned Śāriputra to respond and proclaim [the Dharma]; is this not a failure to discern the faculties [of the listeners]? Answer:
Among those transformed by the Buddhas, there are Bodhisattvas who share the same names. Why, then, should one be surprised by a person?

Those who cling to the Two Vehicles are firm in their attachment to the dharmas they uphold. However, among those of the Two Vehicles, Śāriputra is supreme in wisdom. Now he stands in the presence of the Buddha.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is empty, one should encourage those of the same vehicle [to do likewise]. Realizing that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, one should not cling to them as real.
Furthermore, through the Buddha’s empowerment, one is enabled to understand emptiness and eliminate clinging, lest one fail to reach this goal.

Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
In this passage, the first explanation clarifies the reason why the previously mentioned aggregate of views is empty. Why is this? At that time, the assembly had doubts, thinking:
"All sentient beings perceive and know the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, as being truly existent;

why is it now said that the Bodhisattva perceives them as empty? Therefore, it is now clarified that the five aggregates, such as form, which are grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), are from the very beginning...
Emptiness is non-existent, like the visual distortions of ophthalmia where various forms appear within the void. These forms and the void are one and not two;
the forms grasped through pervasive conceptualization are likewise so. Due to the visual distortion of the fever of afflictions, forms appear within the void of one's own mind.
Yet the nature of these forms is no different from the void; they are entirely non-existent. Therefore, it was said to Śāriputra:
The son of the Licchavis said: "Form is not different from emptiness. If form were truly existent and distinct from emptiness, then the five aggregates would exist within emptiness.
Now, by means of true and correct wisdom, the Bodhisattvas see that the imagined aggregate of form is fundamentally empty and non-existent;
therefore, they say that form is not different from emptiness. Since form is not different from emptiness, how could emptiness itself ever be apprehended?"
Because they are not different, it is said that emptiness is not different from form. Since they do not differ from one another, it is said that form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form.
Form and emptiness are equal and equal; there is no distinction between them. Therefore, one knows that this form is originally empty by nature;
it is not something made empty by the Bodhisattva through forceful contemplation. If form were truly existent and not empty, [it could not be so].
If a bodhisattva forcibly contemplates [the aggregates] as empty, he then falls into perversion (*viparyāsa*). Yet, if ordinary beings perceive reality, they should not be considered perverted;

however, this is not actually the case. Therefore, one knows that form (*rūpa*) is empty, and feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise so.
Just as form and emptiness are non-dual, so too is the principle for the remaining four aggregates.
Śāriputra, this mark of the emptiness of all phenomena is neither born nor extinguished; it is neither defiled nor pure; it neither increases nor decreases.
The second [section] explains the basis for the previous statement on "delivering all from suffering and calamity.

It is precisely because the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are ultimately identical to emptiness and thus devoid of arising, ceasing, and the like, that suffering and calamity likewise do not exist; hence it is said they are "delivered.
Within this passage, there are generally four gates used to reveal how their identity with emptiness constitutes deliverance from calamity. Some say: form...
The fixed nature of all such dharmas exists. Why is this?
These wise ones have variously asserted that dharmas such as form arise from their own essence, or arise from another, or arise from both self and other, or arise without cause;
they thus speak in various ways of the arising of dharmas such as form. For what reason, then, do you say they are empty? Because there is no suffering or affliction. Therefore, now the Buddha...
I tell you, Śāriputra: these dharmas, such as form and the rest, possess only the characteristic of emptiness and have no arising.
If you were to say that dharmas such as form arise from their own intrinsic nature, then a single dharma would possess two natures. This is because:
If it were a single entity alone, there would be no arising. If one says it arises from its own essence, then that essence which acts as the producer must itself have something from which it arises;
thus, there would be two entities. If the producing essence itself has something from which it arises, that which it arises from would be infinite.
If the producing essence has nothing from which it arises, then [arising occurs].
Then there is no arising from [another]. If there is no arising from [another], then there is no arising from self-nature (*svabhāva*).

If there is no arising from self-nature, this means there is no arising by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since arising by way of intrinsic nature does not exist, arising by way of other-nature (*parabhāva*) also does not exist.

Why? Because other-nature exists only in dependence upon intrinsic nature; yet within that "other," there is no such intrinsic nature. Now, since intrinsic nature is absent, other-nature [is likewise absent].
Nor does it exist from both. Therefore, it should not arise from another. If both self-nature and other-nature are absent, then there can be no co-arising.
To say that it arises without a cause is also untenable. Why? Because even arising with a cause has already been refuted.
How much more so, then, could there be arising without a cause?

If there were arising without a cause, then those who practice giving and uphold the precepts would fall into hell, while those who commit the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes would be reborn in heaven, for both cases would equally lack a cause.

If there were truly the arising of form and so forth, one could speak of their cessation; but since there is now no arising of form and so forth, there is likewise no cessation. [This applies] universally.
The self-nature of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as conceived through conceptual construction, lacks both arising and ceasing; how could it not be empty?
Originally, because there was form and so forth, there was suffering and affliction. Now, since form and so forth are empty, one thereby transcends suffering and affliction.

Second is the gate of dispelling defilement and purity to reveal that the characteristics of form and so forth are identical to emptiness. Someone says: "We currently perceive the existence of the out-flowing (*āsrava*)."
All dyed colors and the like arise from defiled causes and conditions; all pure, untainted forms and the like are obtained through undefiled causes and conditions.
Thus, dharmas such as form possess both defilement and purity. Since they possess both defilement and purity, they are not empty.
How can it be said that dharmas such as form are identical to emptiness? Therefore, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says: "If..."
This means that while the fruit does not exist within the conditions, it emerges from those very conditions. Why then does it not emerge from what is not a condition?

For example, since there is no jar within the clay, why does it not emerge from milk? If the fruit were strictly non-existent [within the conditions], there would be neither defilement nor purity, neither suffering nor calamity;
consequently, there would be no distinction between ordinary beings and sages, which would entail the great error of nihilism. [The opponent] replies: "You, sir, merely..."
The eyes afflicted by heat perceive floating flowers in the sky, yet how could they know that these flowers are themselves empty? Thus, the *Madhyamaka* states:
"If an effect arises from various conditions, those conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If conditions lack intrinsic nature, then those conditions do not exist.
Since the self-essence of conditions is non-existent, how can they produce an effect? Therefore, regarding all phenomena such as form—whether defiled or pure—...
The fruit does not arise from conditions, nor does it arise from non-conditions. Since even conditions cannot produce it, how could non-conditions produce it?
If a fruit could be produced by non-conditions, then those who perform wholesome deeds would fall into hell, and those who commit evil deeds would attain rebirth in heaven;
for they would be non-conditions. Since phenomena such as form do not arise from either [of these two], then...
There is no form and so forth; because there is no form and so forth, neither object nor subject of cognition exists. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, like empty space, how could it have defilement or purity?
For example, although it rains for ten thousand years, empty space is not moistened; although a great fire burns it, it is not heated. Why is this? Because its nature is fundamentally..."

Because they are non-existent by nature; that is to say, form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), are fundamentally non-existent. Therefore, defilement and purity are not predicated of them.

Since defilement and purity do not exist, how could there be suffering or calamity? Third is the gate of dispelling increase and decrease, which reveals that form and so forth have the characteristic of being equal to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Someone says: "We see with our own eyes that form and other phenomena increase from causes and conditions to become coarse, and decrease from causes and conditions to become subtle.
Since this increase and decrease from causes and conditions can be observed, they are not empty. Why then do you say that form and all else are empty?
[How can one] transcend all suffering and distress? The answer is: "If it were as your view suggests, it would be like the afflictions..."
Afflicted by craving and thirst, one perceives a mirage as water; yet how could that water be real? It is, in fact, emptiness itself.

Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* establishes [the teaching] to eliminate the distraction of superimposition (*samāropa-vikṣepa*). For this reason, the Sūtra states that "the intrinsic nature of form is empty," and so forth;

this refers to form and other phenomena as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because their intrinsic nature is eternally non-existent. Since form and the rest are eternally non-existent...
How can one say that the subtle increases to become coarse, or that the coarse decreases to become subtle? Since there is neither increase nor decrease, how could there be suffering or calamity?
Therefore, it is said that "one transcends all suffering and calamity."
From here below is the third section, which cites the beginning to categorize the end; this text consists of two parts. First, the citation of the beginning.
Second, from "There is no eye or ear" onwards, is the categorization of the end.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form; there is no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

This refers back to the beginning. Since those preceding sections analyzed the five aggregates—form and so forth—as being uniformly identical to emptiness by means of four gates, one should know that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the following four gates are all of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and are likewise empty.
The reason for this is that [the remaining two natures], the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), [are also empty].
This is fundamentally free from the characteristics of names, words, and conceptual discrimination.
That is to say, the noble sages, in order to provide a point of entry for sentient beings, have provisionally applied adventitious names to all phenomena of the two natures (*dvayadharmatā*).

These applied adventitious names merely serve to exclude one another; however, as for these adventitious names, they ultimately cannot denote the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena. Furthermore, this...
Since all phenomena of the two natures are already devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics, they cannot be taken as objects by any mental activity.
Nevertheless, sentient beings fail to realize that linguistic designations are adventitious and thus conceive of them as fixed and real.

Furthermore, failing to realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, they conceive of fixed and real natures and characteristics as the objects of the mind. In this way, they falsely impute fixed and real names and characteristics.
All these are the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) and are ultimately non-existent, like the son of a barren woman or the hair of a tortoise.

For this reason, they are said to be empty. Since form and so forth that are thoroughly imagined are empty, the principle regarding the thoroughly imagined nature of the twelve bases (āyatana) and so forth in the following four sections is likewise the same.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object.
This second category, the twelve bases (*āyatana*), is empty. As for why these twelve are collectively termed "bases," it is because of these twelve.
Each and every one is capable of acting as a gateway for the growth of consciousness; therefore, they are called "bases" (*āyatana*).
Furthermore, these twelve each possess the meaning of distinct characteristics; for this reason, they are called bases.

Regarding the term "twelve," it refers to the six bases of the faculties—namely, the eye-faculty base up to the mind-faculty base—and the six bases of the objects—namely, the form-object base up to [the dharma-object base].
Up to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is exactly as listed in the sūtras.

The eye has "seeing forms" as its meaning, and so on, up to the mental faculty (*manas*) having "that which is mentally engaged" as its meaning. Such guest-names are all merely conventional designations.

Nevertheless, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), failing to realize their falsity, conceptualize within them a fixed, real nature and differentiation of both names and meanings; this is called "pervasiveness."
Regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): these twelve [bases] are by their very nature empty of the imagined. For this reason they are called "non-existent.
Thus it is said that there is no eye, ear, and so forth, up to and including no form, sound, and so forth.
There is no眼界 (eye-element), and so forth, up to no意識界 (consciousness-element).
This third category is the emptiness of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The reason the eighteen are collectively termed "elements" is because they carry the meaning of seeds (*bīja*).

The seeds of all phenomena within the ālayavijñāna are called "elements" (*dhātu*). Because "element" has the meaning of "cause," and because it can maintain its own nature as well as the nature of cause and effect, it is called an element.
Furthermore, because it maintains the distinct characteristics of all phenomena, it is called an element;
that is to say, although all elements such as earth and so forth differ [in their specific qualities], [they are all termed elements].

There are no others; they are all subsumed within the eighteen [elements]. These eighteen are as follows: the six sense-faculty elements (*ṣaḍ-indriya-dhātu*), namely the eye element up to the mind element;
the six object elements (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya-dhātu*), namely the form element up to the mental-object element, as explained in the section on the bases (*āyatana*);
and the six consciousness elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*), namely the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element. These eighteen are called...

The intrinsic nature and the distinctions of objects are merely conventional designations. Yet, ordinary beings falsely conceive of them as having fixed, real names, intrinsic natures, and distinctions.
These eighteen types of thoroughly imagined attachments are originally empty;
therefore, they are called "non-existent. Thus it is said: "There is no eye-element, and so forth, up to no consciousness-element."
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; likewise, there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.

This fourth category is the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination. These twelve arise in dependence upon conditions, and are therefore called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As for the term "twelve," it refers to ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, and so forth.
Together with birth, aging, and death, these twelve links are subsumed within the realms (dhātus) according to four principles:
namely, at the time of the cause, there is that which projects and that which is projected; and at the time of the fruit, there is that which produces and that which is produced.

Regarding "that which projects at the time of the cause," this refers to ignorance, formations, and consciousness, because the dependent origination has not yet arisen; they now, in the present, perfuse the ālayavijñāna.
The mind is able to project the seeds of beginningless designations, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, thereby enabling them to produce their respective fruits.
What is said to be "projected at the time of the cause" refers to the seeds of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.

Due to the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the preceding ignorance and other factors that have perfumed the mind, they cause name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) to arise sequentially in the future, with each preceding factor depending upon the succeeding one, as the seeds attain growth.
Regarding the statement that "at the time of the fruit they can produce," this refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*);
at the moment of death, these correspond to whichever single karmic latency is concordant with the desire for maturation (*vipāka*).
Because the *vāsanā* (habitual energy) is present before one, it can cause the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth previously projected to bring about their maturation (*vipāka*).
As for the phrase "that which arises at the time of the fruit," this refers to birth, aging, and death.

Because the habitual energy of any single karma conducive to craving—which was previously capable of producing [the result]—is present before one, within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of a single lifetime, it functions just as the name-and-form was previously projected.
The arising of such maturation is termed birth, aging, and death. Now, regarding these twelve links of dependent origination, there are two types of forward order and two types of reverse order;
the intent of this present passage is solely to clarify the two types of forward order.

First is the sequential order of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), which means: conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so on, up to: conditioned by birth (*jāti*) are aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Second is the sequential order of purification (*vyavadāna*), which means: because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; and so on, up to: because birth ceases, aging and death cease.
If one grasps these two types of twelvefold dependent origination—defiled and purified—as having a fixed, real existence of name and referent (*nāma-artha-svabhāva*), [it is an error].
The nature and the specific designations [of these factors] are termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Now, realizing that this defiled twelvefold dependent origination is entirely empty of the imagined nature, it is said: "there is no ignorance," and so on, up to "no old age and death.
Furthermore, realizing that this pure twelvefold dependent origination is also entirely empty of the imagined nature, it is said: "there is no extinction of ignorance," and so on, up to "no..."
The exhaustion of old age and death. Exhaustion is precisely cessation (*nirodha*).
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.

This fifth category is the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths. The reason these four are collectively termed "truths" (*satya*) is that they are examined and verified as real and not false. This is...
Therefore, it is called a "truth" (*satya*). Regarding the term "the truth of suffering": this refers to the birth of sentient beings and the place where they are born.
These two types arise through the power of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), and they are produced by the predominance of karma and afflictions, respectively.
The first two types are both shown to be of the nature of suffering; therefore, they are called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

As for the "Truth of Origination" (*samudaya-satya*), it refers to all karma produced by the predominance of the various afflictions (*kleśa*); these together are called "origination. Because these two types can collectively give rise to the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are called the Truth of Origination.
As for the "Truth of Cessation" (*nirodha-satya*), it refers to [the state] upon the object of focus, True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Because the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are extinguished, it is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). That which is termed the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) refers to the various untainted (*anāsrava*) factors such as ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
because they know suffering, abandon its origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path, their functioning is unimpeded, and thus it is called the Truth of the Path.
If one clings to these four truths as having a fixed, real nature (*svabhāva*), essence, or distinction, this is termed the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*).
Now, having realized that these four [noble truths] are all empty as they are conceptually imputed, it is said that there is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.
Thus far, the first section has clarified that all that is grasped is empty.
"There is no wisdom, nor is there any attainment.
This second line clarifies that the means of realization is also empty. "No wisdom" refers to the emptiness of the observing wisdom;
"no attainment" refers to the emptiness of the observed object. The initial phrase "no wisdom" refers to the *prajñā* that observes the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth.

It is fundamentally free from names, words, and essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). If one grasps at *prajñā* as being a fixed reality, this too is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Now, by dispelling this notion of a fixed nature, wisdom is rendered empty; therefore, it is said that "there is no wisdom.

As for the statement "there is no attainment," it means that the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth—the objects of thorough imagination—are empty from the very beginning, and not [empty] by virtue of the Bodhisattva.
One forcefully contemplates [phenomena] to make them empty; only then does one realize the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that there is "no attainment. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When a bodhisattva practices *prajñā*, they do not grasp at practicing;

they do not grasp at not practicing; they do not grasp at neither practicing nor not practicing; they do not even grasp at non-grasping. This is because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of *prajñā* is unattainable."
Therefore, because the single *dharmatā* is non-existent, it does not follow the movements of phenomena nor does it grasp the characteristics of phenomena.

Furthermore, since the preceding discussion was intended to refute the notion of a fixed, real, and pervasive imagined nature regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, emptiness was employed as a means to dispel that notion.
Fearing that people might take emptiness itself to be the ultimate realized object, it is now being negated.
The realization of this emptiness is likewise not an object to be attained. Thus, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states:
"The Great Sage taught the Dharma of emptiness for the purpose of abandoning all views; yet those who hold emptiness as a view cannot be transformed even by the Buddhas."

Why is this? It was originally because of the existence of illness that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) was borrowed to eliminate it. Once the illness has been eliminated, emptiness also ceases of its own accord.
It is like hail striking down grass: when the grass dies, the hail dissolves. If it were otherwise, one would abandon existence and grasp at non-existence;

this would be like fleeing from a mountain peak only to rush into a valley—neither would escape suffering. How, then, could one find peace for oneself? Thus far, we have relied on the method of "expelling" [the afflictions].
The preceding section elucidated *prajñā* by way of the gate of causes;
from here on, the second section elucidates *prajñā* by way of the gate of fruits through reliance on manifest realization. As for the cause, it is without dependence and without attainment;
as for the fruit, it is without marks. This markless *prajñā* has never existed as either cause or fruit, yet for the sake of transforming sentient beings, it is provisionally [established].
This is explained by way of the terminology of cause and effect. Within this passage, there are further two parts: first, it clarifies that one attains nirvāṇa by relying on prajñā;
second, it clarifies that one attains bodhi by relying on prajñā. This too is merely a provisional expression stating that one attains bodhi by relying on prajñā.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, the Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in the mind.
Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, one attains ultimate Nirvāṇa.

Within the preceding section there are five parts. First, it reiterates the previous point to introduce the subsequent one; hence it says, "Because there is nothing to be apprehended. Second, it clarifies the person who relies [upon the practice];
hence it says, "Bodhisattva. Third, it clarifies the Prajñā upon which they rely. Fourth, it clarifies the opening of the gate of liberation.
Fifth, it correctly clarifies the realization and attainment of liberation. Of these, the first three have already been explained previously. The fourth clarifies the opening [of the gate].
Regarding the "gate of liberation": "being without obstruction" refers to the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
This means that by realizing that all phenomena are empty of self, other, and both, the wisdom that contemplates them is not obstructed by the notion of intrinsic existence.

As for the statement, "because there is no obstruction, there is no fear," this clarifies the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). It is because one has realized that all phenomena are [empty of] self and other...
Because both are empty, one knows that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are without marks (*animitta*).

The reason for this is that if one does not know that all phenomena are without marks, one is externally obstructed by marks and internally experiences much fear. If one realizes that all phenomena are without marks, one is not externally obstructed by marks and internally there is no fear.
"Far removed from inverted dreams and delusions" clarifies the liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The gates of liberation: because one realizes that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is no external obstruction by signs and no internal fear;
thus, one understands that all phenomena are merely inversions, like dreams—illusory and unreal—and therefore remains detached, giving rise to no further aspiration or seeking.
"Ultimate nirvāṇa" precisely clarifies the fruit of liberation: the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness mentioned above.
However, this is the gateway to liberation through which one enters the state of ultimate nirvāṇa and liberation. One may thus be free from all obstructions.
By clearly realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), because one has attained the understanding that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, wisdom is unimpeded.
By being free from fear, one clearly realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), as one no longer conceives of a self.

Therefore, being inwardly free from fear and far removed from inversion reiterates the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Being far removed from dreams and illusions reiterates the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Because one has attained mastery over these two types of emptiness such that no further burdens remain, one is able to ultimately realize *nirvāṇa*.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, an unequaled mantra.
It is able to eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false. Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken.
The third section is the extensive praise that reveals its excellence. This passage contains three parts. First, the four lines provide the direct praise.
Because it relies upon *prajñā*, one is able to counteract the two types of grasping and realize the two fruits; therefore, we know that *prajñā* is a "great mantra," and so forth.
Generally, that which constitutes a mantra is so called because it extinguishes evil and generates goodness; it can dissolve the enmity of the four Māras. Therefore, it is said to be "great."
This divine mantra can destroy the two kinds of delusive obscurations; therefore, it is called the "Great Illuminating Mantra. These two praises indicate its ability to extinguish evil.
Among all that is wholesome, there is nothing superior to this; therefore, it is called the "Unsurpassed Mantra.
The Buddha is the most honored among all sages and is thus named "Incomparable" (asama). Since he is born from Prajñā, Prajñā is named "Equal to the Incomparable" (asamasama). Therefore—
The Sūtra says: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.

This first pair of praises [the eternality of the Dharma and the Buddhas] extols that which can produce goodness; the second pair [the removal of suffering and the realization of the two truths] explains the intent of these praises by stating that they can eliminate all suffering and realize the two realities.
Since these matters are not false, they are praised as divine mantras and so forth. Third, "Therefore, it is said... concludes that.
The reason why Prajñā is designated as a mantra (dhāraṇī) is precisely because it possesses the four aforementioned meanings of destroying evil and giving rise to goodness;
therefore, Prajñā is called a mantra.
The mantra is spoken as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi*.
"Svāhā. This fourth section reiterates the preceding sūtra and extols it to manifest its excellence; thus, the sūtra itself is named a mantra.
It is not that there is a separate mantra apart from the sūtra. For example, the Ṣaṇmukha-dhāraṇī-mantra still subsumes the preceding sūtra and constitutes six [sections].

This is merely a gateway. Since the sutras are treated as mantras, every character within the words of these sutra-mantras is empowered by the majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
each individual word and phrase also encompasses manifold meanings.

If these were translated here into the words of our local dialect, they might be increased or decreased, resulting in a deficiency of meaning and failing to produce the efficacious results of recitation. For this reason, [they are not translated].
Alternatively, when addressing spirits, deities, or animals, the speech used often does not conform to the standard terminology of India;
for this reason, it is left untranslated. This is precisely why the mantras found throughout the various sūtras are all left untranslated as well.
